Problems

1. SQL-injection bug  
   request.params.id is copied straight into the query string.  
   If the caller sends /users/1;DROP TABLE users-- the final text becomes  
   SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 1;DROP TABLE users--  LIMIT 1  
   – the whole database is now at the mercy of the attacker.

2. Wrong / fragile quoting  
   The query is being built with … id = " + id + " … (double quotes).  
   • Most SQL dialects expect single quotes around string literals, not double.  
   • id is supposed to be an integer, so it should not be quoted at all.  
   • When id contains a quote the statement breaks.

3. Input not validated / typed  
   There is no guarantee id is an integer ≥ 1.  
   Non-numeric or negative values will throw SQL errors or return unintended rows.

4. SELECT * information disclosure  
   * returns every column, including password_hash, password_salt, reset_tokens, etc.  
   An attacker that finds an IDOR or an SQLi will receive much more data than needed.

5. Maintainability / performance  
   • Using * means every schema change affects every caller.  
   • Extra columns increase network payload and cache‐miss rates.

6. Logic bug masqueraded by LIMIT 1  
   LIMIT 1 hides data-integrity problems (duplicate ids) instead of preventing them.

How to fix

A. Use a parameterised / prepared statement – never string concatenation.

   // Example with Node + mysql2
   const id = Number.parseInt(req.params.id, 10);
   if (!Number.isInteger(id) || id <= 0) {
     return next(new Error('Invalid user id'));
   }

   const [rows] = await pool.execute(
     'SELECT id, username, email FROM users WHERE id = ?',
     [id]
   );

   // pg driver
   const { rows } = await client.query(
     'SELECT id, username, email FROM users WHERE id = $1',
     [id]
   );

B. Validate & sanitise input before it reaches the database layer.

   • Convert to the expected type (parseInt / Number).  
   • Reject NaN, negative, or out-of-range values early.  
   • Consider using a schema-validation library (Joi, Yup, zod, class-validator, …).

C. Fetch only the columns you really need.

   SELECT id, username, email FROM users WHERE id = ?;

   This enforces least-privilege and cuts bandwidth.

D. Enforce a UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint on users.id in the database so duplicates are impossible; then you do not need LIMIT 1.

E. Error handling  
   Wrap DB calls in try/catch and return generic error messages; do not leak raw SQL errors to the client.

F. Principle of least privilege  
   The DB user used by the application should have only SELECT rights on the users table (not DROP, DELETE, etc.) if the application never needs them.

Summary

Replace string concatenation with parameterised queries, validate/escape all input, select explicit columns, and enforce proper database constraints. That removes the SQL-injection vulnerability, avoids quoting bugs, limits data exposure, and improves maintainability and performance.
